title: Hubble's sharpest view of the Orion Nebula
caption: The Orion Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 42, Messier 43, Orion Nebula · constellation Orion · about 1400 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, M. Robberto ( Space Telescope Science Institute/ESA) and the Hubble Space Telescope Orion Treasury Project Team

recognition.text: Ranked #21 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A vast hollow of churning gas and dust fills the frame, sculpted into what look like plateaus, ridges and valleys, and sprinkled with more than 3,000 stars of many sizes. This is the Orion Nebula, the closest star-forming region to Earth, in the sharpest view Hubble had ever made of it. Some of its stars had never before been spotted in visible light.

The bright center holds the Trapezium, the nebula's four most massive stars, named for the four-sided pattern they make. Their ultraviolet light is hollowing out the cloud and stunting the growth of hundreds of smaller neighbors. Close by sit young stars still wrapped in disks of material, the raw ingredients of planetary systems, though they are too small to pick out at this scale.
Near the bottom, faint red points are brown dwarfs, objects too small to sustain nuclear fusion in their cores like the Sun. Hubble caught them in visible light for the first time.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (30.03 x 30.03 arcminutes) and distance (1400 light years), the frame spans roughly 12 × 12 light-years. Its light set out about 1,400 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This mosaic comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using filters that span visible light and the near-infrared, including one that isolates the red glow of hydrogen. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The eye cannot see the near-infrared part of this data, and Hubble's long exposures record faint stars and brown dwarfs far too dim to see directly.

behind.people: See full credit: NASA, ESA, M. Robberto ( Space Telescope Science Institute/ESA) and the Hubble Space Telescope Orion Treasury Project Team
behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: At upper left glows M43, often called a miniature Orion Nebula because a single massive young star shapes it, rather than four. Dark pillars beside it point toward the Trapezium and are holding out against its erosive ultraviolet light. To the right, arcs and bubbles mark where winds of charged particles from the Trapezium stars slam into surrounding material.
The picture combines 520 Hubble images in five colors with ground-based photos, and the mosaic spans roughly the apparent size of the full Moon.
alt: A glowing cloud of dust and gas scattered with thousands of stars, bright at the center, with a smaller glow at upper left, dark pillars, and faint red stars near the bottom.
